title: Not a spade (Avot 4:5)
hookLine: Tzadok: don't make Torah a crown to show off or a spade to dig with
carry: not a crown, not a spade
tomorrow: a dropped book, and a kiss. why?

cards: A résumé line, a debate won, a fact dropped at dinner to look sharp: knowing things is handy. Rabbi Tzadok says: don't make the words of Torah a crown to make yourself great with, or a spade to dig with.
And Hillel, the mishnah adds, used to say: whoever makes use of the crown passes away.

teach.b: So here's the question: what is learning for? Tzadok's two pictures cover the two temptations.
A crown is status: learning worn so people look up at you. A spade is income: learning used to dig out a living or a win.
Both turn the Torah into a tool, and Hillel's line warns that a tool used that way wears out its user. The tradition's word for the other way is lishmah, for its own sake.
A Buddhist neighbor says something close, in the Majjhima Nikaya.

teach.h: THE SNAKE GRABBED BY THE TAIL.
teach.b: The Buddha describes people who learn his teaching only to criticize others or win arguments, and compares them to someone who grabs a water snake by the tail: it turns and bites.
The shared point: knowledge held for the wrong reason hurts the one holding it. One honest difference: in the same talk, the Buddha calls his teaching a raft, for crossing over, not for holding onto.
Avot doesn't set the Torah down after the crossing.

teach.h: A RAFT, OR TURN IT AND TURN IT.
teach.b: Ben Bag Bag says to turn it and turn it, for everything is in it.

teach.h: NOT A CROWN, NOT A SPADE.
teach.b: Keep it, Tzadok says; just don't wield it.

how: Jews speak of Torah lishmah, learning for its own sake, as an ideal; Avot 4:5 is a classic source for not using learning for status or gain.

s: Tzadok only warns against earning money from Torah

games.q: a coworker keeps dropping philosophy quotes in meetings, mostly to make others look slow. by Tzadok's line, what's off?
o: the learning has become a crown, used to make himself big.
nothing; knowledge is meant to win the room.
he should quote less well-known books.
games.why: Tzadok: not a crown to make yourself great with. Hillel adds that whoever uses the crown passes away.

practice: Close your eyes and choose one thing you know and love, a story, a song, a verse, a skill, for no reason except that you love it. Turn it over in your mind for the length of the sit: not to use it, not to show it, just to hold it.

wordCard.voice: Not a spade. Tzadok's kardom: learning isn't a tool for digging out status or money.

orig.note: Hebrew: an axe or spade; Tzadok's picture of learning used as a tool.

carryVoice: Here's your line: not a crown, not a spade, just the thing itself, for its own sake. Good night, or good morning.
